reviews.title: MISLEADING ADVERTISING AND DENIED REFUND!
reviews.text:
I rarely leave negative reviews, but I feel obligated to warn others before they waste their money the way I did.

I purchased this app for $39 because the advertising clearly gives the impression that it can measure blood pressure by placing your finger over your phone’s camera. The screenshots and promotional images strongly suggest that the app can provide actual blood pressure readings using the phone alone. That’s what convinced me to buy it.

After purchasing and installing the app, I quickly discovered that it does not actually do what the advertisement led me to believe it could do. The marketing and the actual functionality are two very different things.

As soon as I realized this, I immediately requested a refund. My request was denied. I then appealed the decision, explaining that the advertising was misleading and that I purchased the app based on those claims. That appeal was also denied.

So now I’m out $39 for an app that did not deliver what its advertising appeared to promise.

My biggest concern isn’t even the money. It’s that other consumers may see the same advertisements, believe the same claims, and end up making the same mistake. Health-related apps should be especially clear and transparent about what they can and cannot do. Consumers should not have to discover the limitations only after paying.

reviews.title: Misleading Marketing at Its Worst
reviews.text:
The Hook: A False Promise
This app is marketed with bold, high-tech claims: "Your iPhone now supports blood pressure monitoring" and "Blood pressure for Apple Watch." For anyone looking to manage their cardiovascular health, this sounds like a revolutionary breakthrough. The advertising leads you to believe that by simply using the sensors on your phone or watch, you can get an instant systolic and diastolic reading.
The Reality: A Manual Logbook in Disguise
The deception only becomes clear once you’ve already downloaded the app or dug deep into the FAQ, where it explicitly states:
"No, the app does not measure blood pressure. You can manually log these values after measuring them with a compatible device."

There is a massive difference between monitoring (the act of measuring) and tracking (the act of typing in numbers). This app is essentially a digital notebook that charges you for a feature your iPhone’s built-in "Health" app already provides for free.
The Trap: Financial Friction
The most frustrating part of this experience isn't just the misleading "bait-and-switch" marketing—it’s the difficulty of getting your money back. Even after canceling immediately upon realizing the app cannot perform the physical task of measuring blood pressure, Apple’s refund system often denies these claims because "the app functions as described" in the fine print.
Final Verdict
